sentences.text: Eremosuchus is an extinct animal belonging to the group of sebecosuchian notosuchians.
The species is named E. elkoholicus, and its defining specimen is a single dentary bone measuring 156 mm in length.
In adults, the two halves of this lower jaw diverged by about 10 to 15 degrees, whereas juveniles showed a wider gap of 15 to 20 degrees.
This bone held 12 tooth sockets arranged in a full row, with the front teeth angled forward due to the orientation of their sockets.
The lower half of the fibula curves backward in a way unique to this animal, while the vertebrae are amphicoelous with rounded bottoms and noticeable narrowing.
Prominent parallel ridges cover about one-third of the underside of the tail vertebrae.
Its teeth were serrated and blade-like, a feature known as ziphodonty that may have changed as the animal grew.
The backward curve of the fibula is a unique trait not seen in other related crocodylomorphs.
This predator lived in a shallow lake environment that experienced periodic drying and occasional high-energy water inflows.
Remains were found in 1982 at the El Kohol site in northern Algeria by researchers from the Université d'Oran, Sorbonne Universités, and Université de Montpellier.
Buffetaut first described the animal in 1989 based on isolated cranial and postcranial material, and Nicholl and colleagues published a redescription in 2025.
The serrated, blade-like teeth suggest a specific feeding strategy that might have shifted from juvenile to adult stages.
A gap between the seventh and eighth dentary teeth in the juvenile specimen could be a shared feature or simply individual variation.
However, researchers question whether tooth diameter is a reliable indicator of size because the holotype is poorly preserved.
It is currently the only named sebecid known from continental Africa and may link South American and European taxa.
In 1989, Eric Buffetaut classified the genus in the family Trematochampsidae, though this assignment has been challenged.
Eremosuchus lived during the Ypresian stage of the Early Eocene, between 56 and 48.07 million years ago.
It is debated whether Eremosuchus's lineage split off during sebecid dispersal between South America and Europe, or if ancestors arrived in North Africa from Europe via the Tethys Sea.

Researchers suggest that the variation in tooth enamel ornamentation might be due to individual or species-level variation rather than distinct species, while it is also debated whether multiple types of osteoderm ornamentation belong to the species or if neither type belongs to Eremosuchus.
Turner and Calvo argued that the features used to assign Eremosuchus to Trematochampsidae were of questionable value.
